THE RECEIVER

Where the numbers come from.

Follow a signal

Light travels about 300 metres in one microsecond. The receiver multiplies the time it measures by the speed of light.

True time in flight
Time on the phone’s clock
Apparent distance

Crowd the sky

Give both skies the same small errors. When the satellites look at the phone from similar directions, those errors can move the fix farther.

Satellite arrangement

Bounce one signal

A signal that bounces off a building can reach the phone late. Compare the same six readings with and without an echo on S6.

Show the actual readings and solver updates

Each measurement gives apparent distance = distance to satellite + clock bias. The receiver starts from a survey origin, predicts the readings, and repeatedly adjusts its guess to reduce the squared differences.

HDOP describes horizontal uncertainty per metre of independent, equal-variance range noise. The green and blue markers use the same simulated ground coordinates.

What the model simplifies

The city, route and satellite positions are simulated. The scene compresses orbital distances and the height axis. Calculations use straight-line distances in three dimensions and a spherical orbit shell at GPS altitude. The model leaves out atmospheric delays, satellite-clock corrections, Earth rotation during signal flight and radio acquisition.

The trail shows a sampled nearby branch. Its slider changes the proposed receiver clock while the three recorded measurements stay fixed. GPS’s full solve receives satellite positions and measured ranges alone.
